## Proposition 10.92
**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a second apotome, the âsideâ of the area is a first apotome of a medial straight line.

**Step 1.** Let the area be contained by the rational straight line AC and the second apotome AD. I say that the "side" of the area AC·AD is a first apotome of a medial straight line. Let DG be the annex to AD; then AG is the whole of the second apotome. By the definition of a second apotome (D10.3.2), DG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out, sq(AG) is greater than sq(DG) by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AG, and AG is incommensurable in length with the assigned rational straight line. Since AC is rational and AD is a second apotome, let us proceed to find the "side" of the rectangle AC·AD.

**Step 2.** Let DG be the annex to AD, so that AG is the whole. By D10.3.2 the annex DG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AC (since AC is rational and serves as the assigned rational line), while AG is incommensurable in length with AC. Also sq(AG) > sq(DG) by the square on a line commensurable in length with AG.

**Step 3.** Apply the rectangle AC·AG to AC, producing the breadth AG as width; similarly AC·DG to AC producing DG as width. The rectangle AC·AD equals the rectangle AC·AG minus the rectangle AC·DG (since AD = AG - DG). Since DG is commensurable in length with AC, and both are rational, the rectangle AC·DG is rational (by 10.19). Since AG is incommensurable in length with AC, and both are rational (commensurable in square with AC), the rectangle AC·AG is medial (by 10.21).

**Step 4.** Bisect DG at E, and to AG apply a rectangle equal to the square on EG and deficient by a square figure; let this rectangle be the rectangle AH·HG. Since sq(AG) > sq(DG) by the square on a line commensurable with AG (by the definition of second apotome), and the rectangle applied equals sq(EG) = (1/4)sq(DG), by 10.17 the segments AH and HG are commensurable in length.

**Step 5.** Describe a semicircle on AG with diameter AG, draw HK perpendicular to AG at H meeting the semicircle at K, and join AK, GK. Since the angle AKG is in a semicircle, the angle AKG is right (by 3.31). Since AH and HG are commensurable in length (Step 4), by 6.17 the rectangle AH·HG equals sq(KH), and by the relation sq(AK) = AH·AG and sq(GK) = GH·GA (from the right triangle and 6.8, or equivalently 2.14 and the properties of the semicircle), the squares on AK and GK can be analyzed.

**Step 6.** From the right triangle AKG with altitude KH, we have sq(AK) = AH·AG and sq(GK) = HG·GA (by 6.8 and the perpendicular from K to the diameter). Now AH is commensurable in length with HG (Step 4), so sq(AK) : sq(GK) = AH : HG (by 6.1), and therefore sq(AK) is commensurable with sq(GK). Thus AK is commensurable with GK in square (by 10.11).

**Step 7.** Since sq(AK) + sq(GK) = sq(AG) (by 1.47, as angle AKG is right), and AG is rational and incommensurable in length with AC, sq(AG) is a rational area but incommensurable with sq(AC). Now sq(AK) + sq(GK) = sq(AG). Since AG is incommensurable in length with AC, and sq(AG) = sq(AK) + sq(GK), the sum sq(AK) + sq(GK) equals the square on AG, which is rational in the sense of being commensurable with the square on AG. However, AG is rational (commensurable in square with AC) but incommensurable in length with AC, so sq(AG) is medial with respect to AC. Therefore sq(AK) + sq(GK) is medial (by 10.23 and 10.15, since sq(AK) and sq(GK) are commensurable and their sum is medial).

**Step 8.** Now the rectangle AK·GK: since sq(AK) = AH·AG and sq(GK) = HG·AG, we have 2·rect(AK, GK) = 2·KH·AG (from the altitude relation, but more precisely: rect(AK, GK)^2 = sq(AK)·sq(GK) = AH·AG·HG·AG = AH·HG·sq(AG)). Instead, note that the rectangle AC·AD = AC·AG - AC·DG, and from the semicircle construction, rect(AC, AD) = sq(AK') where AK' is the "side" we seek. We use the identity: since DG = 2·EG, rect(AC, DG) = 2·rect(AC, EG). Also, rect(AH, HG) = sq(EG) (from the application in Step 4 and the bisection), so sq(KH) = rect(AH, HG) = sq(EG), hence KH = EG.

**Step 9.** More directly: the rectangle AC·AD is the area whose "side" we seek. Apply this rectangle to a line to form a square; let the side of that square be denoted w. Following the standard construction of 10.54-10.59 and 10.91, set the problem up as follows. We have already that rect(AC, AG) is medial (Step 3) and rect(AC, DG) is rational (Step 3). We need two lines whose squares sum to rect(AC, AG) and whose product rectangle equals (1/2)·rect(AC, DG).

**Step 10.** Produce the rectangle AC·AG to get a medial area, and take the rectangle AC·DG which is rational. On a line FG equal to AC, apply the area rect(AC, AG) as a square on some line, or rather, following the approach of 10.91 more closely: Let MN and NO be straight lines such that sq(MN) + sq(NO) = rect(AC, AG) and rect(MN, NO) = (1/2)·rect(AC, DG). Then sq(MN) + sq(NO) is medial and rect(MN, NO) is rational.

**Step 11.** Since sq(MN) + sq(NO) is medial (it equals rect(AC, AG), which is medial by Step 3), and 2·rect(MN, NO) is rational (it equals rect(AC, DG), which is rational by Step 3), and the medial area sq(MN) + sq(NO) is incommensurable with the rational area 2·rect(MN, NO) (since a medial area is incommensurable with a rational area, by the definitions D10.1.3 and D10.1.4), the conditions match those of 10.34 and 10.74.

**Step 12.** We verify that MN and NO are medial and commensurable in square only. Since AH and HG are commensurable in length (Step 4), and sq(MN) = rect(AC, AH) and sq(NO) = rect(AC, HG), where AC is rational, we need AH and HG to be rational. Since AG is rational (it is commensurable in square with AC) and AH, HG are parts of AG with AH commensurable with HG, but AG is incommensurable in length with AC. Now rect(AC, AH) and rect(AC, HG) are the squares on MN and NO respectively. Since AH is incommensurable in length with AC (because AG is incommensurable in length with AC, and AH is a part of AG commensurable with AG by 10.15), the rectangle AC·AH is medial (by 10.21). Thus sq(MN) is medial, so MN is medial (by D10.1.4). Similarly sq(NO) is medial, so NO is medial.

**Step 13.** Since sq(MN) = rect(AC, AH) and sq(NO) = rect(AC, HG), we have sq(MN) : sq(NO) = AH : HG (by 6.1). Since AH is commensurable with HG (Step 4), sq(MN) is commensurable with sq(NO) (by 10.6). Therefore MN is commensurable with NO in square. Since sq(MN) + sq(NO) is medial and 2·rect(MN, NO) is rational, MN and NO are incommensurable in square with each other only, not in length (if they were commensurable in length, then sq(MN) + sq(NO) would have a fixed ratio to rect(MN, NO), making the medial commensurable with the rational, which is impossible by 10.26). So MN and NO are commensurable in square only.

**Step 14.** Since MN and NO are medial straight lines commensurable in square only, and they contain a rational rectangle (rect(MN, NO) is rational), the difference MN - NO is a first apotome of a medial straight line (by 10.74, which defines the first apotome of a medial straight line as the remainder when from a medial straight line is subtracted a medial straight line commensurable in square only and containing with it a rational rectangle).

**Step 15.** It remains to show that MN - NO is indeed the "side" of the rectangle AC·AD. We have sq(MN) + sq(NO) = rect(AC, AG) and 2·rect(MN, NO) = rect(AC, DG). Then sq(MN) + sq(NO) - 2·rect(MN, NO) = rect(AC, AG) - rect(AC, DG) = rect(AC, AG - DG) = rect(AC, AD). But sq(MN) + sq(NO) - 2·rect(MN, NO) = sq(MN - NO) (by 2.7). Therefore sq(MN - NO) = rect(AC, AD), so MN - NO is the "side" of the area contained by AC and AD.

**Step 16.** Therefore the "side" of the area contained by the rational straight line AC and the second apotome AD is a first apotome of a medial straight line. Q.E.D.

heath_proof_text: For let the area AB be contained by the rational straight line AC and the second apotome AD; I say that the “side” of the area AB is a first apotome of a medial straight line. For let DG be the annex to AD; therefore AG, GD are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, [X. 73] and the annex DG is commensurable with the rational straight line AC set out, while the square on the whole AG is greater than the square on the annex GD by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AG. [X. Deff. III. 2] Since then the square on AG is greater than the square on GD by the square on a straight line commensurable with AG, therefore, if there be applied to AG a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on GD and deficient by a square figure, it divides it into commensurable parts. [X. 17] Let then DG be bisected at E, let there be applied to AG a parallelogram equal to the square on EG and deficient by a square figure, and let it be the rectangle AF, FG; therefore AF is commensurable in length with FG. Therefore AG is also commensurable in length with each of the straight lines AF, FG. [X. 15] But AG is rational and incommensurable in length with AC; therefore each of the straight lines AF, FG is also rational and incommensurable in length with AC; [X. 13] therefore each of the rectangles AI, FK is medial. [X. 21] Again, since DE is commensurable with EG, therefore DG is also commensurable with each of the straight lines DE, EG. [X. 15] But DG is commensurable in length with AC. Therefore each of the rectangles DH, EK is rational. [X. 19] Let then the square LM be constructed equal to AI, and let there be subtracted NO equal to FK and being about the same angle with LM, namely the angle LPM; therefore the squares LM, NO are about the same diameter. [VI. 26] Let PR be their diameter, and let the figure be drawn. Since then AI, FK are medial and are equal to the squares on LP, PN, the squares on LP, PN are also medial; therefore LP, PN are also medial straight lines commensurable in square only. And, since the rectangle AF, FG is equal to the square on EG, therefore, as AF is to EG, so is EG to FG, [VI. 17] while, as AF is to EG, so is AI to EK, and, as EG is to FG, so is EK to FK; [VI. 1] therefore EK is a mean proportional between AI, FK. [V. 11] But MN is also a mean proportional between the squares LM, NO, and AI is equal to LM, and FK to NO; therefore MN is also equal to EK. But DH is equal to EK, and LO equal to MN; therefore the whole DK is equal to the gnomon UVW and NO. Since then the whole AK is equal to LM, NO, and, in these, DK is equal to the gnomon UVW and NO, therefore the remainder AB is equal to TS. But TS is the square on LN; therefore the square on LN is equal to the area AB; therefore LN is the “side” of the area AB. I say that LN is a first apotome of a medial straight line. For, since EK is rational and is equal to LO, therefore LO, that is, the rectangle LP, PN, is rational. But NO was proved medial; therefore LO is incommensurable with NO. But, as LO is to NO, so is LP to PN; [VI. 1] therefore LP, PN are incommensurable in length. [X. 11] Therefore LP, PN are medial straight lines commensurable in square only which contain a rational rectangle; therefore LN is a first apotome of a medial straight line. [X. 74] And it is the “side” of the area AB. Therefore the “side” of the area AB is a first apotome of a medial straight line.
